lines.text: Do you know how a lighthouse throws its light so far? The secret isn't the lamp. It's the giant glass around it.
Early lighthouses burned fires or oil lamps, and most of that light just spilled into the sky, or down into the ground.
In 1822, a French physicist called Augustin Fresnel designed a new kind of lens. Rings of glass prisms, stacked around the light.
Each ring bends the light a little, so rays heading up or down all turn, and leave in one flat, bright beam.
It works like a huge, thick lens, cut into slices. Far thinner and lighter, but just as strong.
The lens turns, so ships see flashes. And every lighthouse has its own pattern, like two flashes every ten seconds, printed on sea charts.
So sailors can read a dark coastline like a map.
